utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Defence for Simo Zaric, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam Presiding Officer. Good morning to all in this courtroom. Mr. Tubakovic, before I put a couple of questions to you, let me just give you some instructions as to the best way to proceed so that whatever you tell us today is correctly recorded in the transcript. So when I put my question to you, wait for a couple of seconds before answering, and don't hurry so that the interpreters can accurately interpret everything you say, which is very important for the record. Will you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Marko Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me when you were born.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of January, 1938.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where are you residing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am living in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete your elementary education?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: In my native village, Gornja Slatina, near Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete your secondary education and which kind of school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the teachers college in Derventa and the university for teachers training in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is your status today?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am currently retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Have you served in the Yugoslav People's Army? When and where?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: A long time ago, yes, I did serve in the Yugoslav People's Army, from October 1958 until September 1959. Half of that service was in Zadar in Croatia, and the other half in Cacak in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you completed your military service in the JNA, did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I served in the School of Officers in Reserve for the artillery, and upon completion I acquired the rank of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you married?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have two sons and two grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us for how many years you have been living in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have been living in Bosanski Samac ever since 1972, which makes it about 27 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us now what rank in the Yugoslav People's Army as a reserve officer you had in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 I had been a major for some ten years already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what rank do you have now?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have the same rank; I am a major. So since the war, I was not promoted in the military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So your current rank is the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The same rank I had in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And that was a rank you acquired as an officer in reserve. Of which army?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now it is the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know Mr. Tihic, as we lived in the same town, so I know him well, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Zaric as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet a person nicknamed Bokan?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Bokan? No, I never met any such person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In the period from the 18th of April, 1992 up until the 26th of April, 1992 did you go to the police station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: In that period I wasn't in Samac at all, so I couldn't have been in the police station either, so I was not in the police station in that period. In fact, I don't remember that I ever entered the police station throughout the war. As for the beginning, I certainly didn't because I just wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you transferred to the command of the 2nd Bosnian Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Bosnian Infantry Brigade came into existence on the 20th of May, 1992, and I was one of the first officers to join that command when it was formed, because up until then it was a tactical group of the Yugoslav People's Army, the so-called 17th Tactical Group. And in view of the fact that from that date on the Yugoslav People's Army ceased to operate in that territory, the Army of Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed and the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, which had the same zone of responsibility as the tactical group. So I remember that date very well; it was on the 20th of May when I went to that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the commander of that 2nd Bosnian Infantry Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the day when the commanders changed. The outgoing commander of the tactical group, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic left the territory and went to Serbia, and his place as commander of the 2nd Bosnian Brigade was taken by Colonel Mihajlo Djurdjevic, who originally came from the municipality of Samac and he came to serve there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska after Colonel Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, it was Dragan Djordjevic, nicknamed Crni, who was appointed. And after him, I think it was Radovanovic. And after that, it was Mile Beronja, who took over in August 1992. There were several changes in the period between May and August.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So throughout that period of 1992 you were a member of the command of the 2nd Infantry Brigade. Can you tell us, please, what was the function that you held in the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the position of Assistant Chief of Staff for Recruitment and Personnel Affairs. That was my duty according to establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you recollect - and please tell us in you do - when the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade was joined by Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric joined -- I'm not sure of the date, but I think it was in September 1992. In the course of September 1992 he came as a member of the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what post and function did Mr. Simo Zaric perform when he joined the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was assigned to the post of Assistant Commander for Morale, Religious and Legal Affairs. That was the name of the position according to establishment, for Morale, Legal and Religious Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And can you tell us how many members the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska had?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The top command staff consisted of about 15 members, I think. By establishment there should have been up to 15 posts, but I'm not quite sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did the command come to the conclusion that it was necessary to draw up a report on negative effects on the morale of the army of the 2nd Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The command felt it necessary to examine the state of morale in the units and on the basis of that examination within the brigade and in the zone of responsibility of the brigade to analyse that information and any causes undermining morale with a view to improving it because we felt that there were some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, who was assigned by the command to prepare that analysis?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: According to establishment, that was the main duty of the Assistant Commander for Morale, Legal and Religious Affairs, which means of Simo Zaric, and he was one of the key persons who worked on the analysis of the situation and the drafting of the report. Of course, he was assisted by other members of the command in doing this; among them, I was one, as one of the links in the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And was this report studied, reviewed by the command, and was there a discussion on it among the command members?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The report was thoroughly prepared, and once the text had been drafted, the command reviewed it on a number of occasions and finally - and I think this was towards the end of November 1992 - that the command officially at a meeting of the command adopted the text unanimously. The members of the command adopted this report unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When this report or information memo was adopted, were members of the East Bosnian Corps present?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the report was being finally adopted, the command meeting was attended by two officers of the command of the East Bosnian Corps, the Assistant Commander for Morale, and the head of the security of the corps. I think their names were Jakovljevic and Dosev, and those officers were present. And as far as I can remember, they spoke with praise of the maturity of the command and commended it for having had the strength to analyse the situation and frankly state certain tendencies which were undermining the morale in the unit and generally affecting the political situation in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After this report was adopted, what did the command members do? Did they sign it, or what happened? Could you describe the procedure for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Once the report was adopted, all command members, including the commander, headed by the commander, signed the report themselves, which in fact confirms our unanimous adoption of it. And the main conclusion of the command staff at the time was that all the matters covered by this report, especially these various negative tendencies that were emerging, that within the activities of the subordinate units of the 2nd Posavina Brigade efforts be made to overcome shortcomings but without sort of mentioning that any such report existed, as the members of the command were familiar what the problems were, that efforts with done to overcome them. And all the present command members adopted this report and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally sign it as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I adopted it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown on the screen the first and last page of this report, please. It is P127, Exhibit P127.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And the last page now, please, with the signatures. Mr. Tubakovic, please have a look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: My name appears under number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is the same signature I affixed today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need this exhibit on the screen any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you recollect what happened after that? Were there any meetings, with whom, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the report dealt in addition to the state of morale in the units but also with the overall situation and conditions in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, as far as I can now recollect, certain negative tendencies were identified, both with respect to the civilian authorities. And after a couple of days, maybe two or three, but very shortly after this -- now, how this report reached the civilian authorities, I don't know, but I do know that there was dissatisfaction among certain elements in the authorities and they requested to have a meeting with the command and that meeting was indeed held, and there were very fervent debates as to certain tendencies that had been mentioned in the report and representatives of the civilian authorities were not at all pleased that we had described the overall situation in that way and expressed our dissatisfaction with those negative tendencies. So there was a meeting attended by the most responsible figures from the civilian authorities and members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who attended that meeting on behalf of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was the President of the Municipality, the President of the Executive Council, the Chief of the Public Security Station, the people with the highest positions, also members of the executive council. Among others, there was someone who was not from our area. I think he came from a republic level, SUP or MUP, somebody called Ninic, as far as I can remember the surname. And the others I knew personally, except for him, who I met for the first time on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how did the meeting end?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the meeting ended by them having expressed very sharp dissatisfaction of what the report contained, and it was stated that the contents of that report should not be publicised. Conditionally speaking, I don't know how to put it, they were dissatisfied and angry that we had highlighted these phenomena because they were within their spheres of responsibility, within the civilian sphere of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So did that meeting end in some sort of an agreement, a common agreement, or did everything remain open, outstanding?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The loudest criticism and the most serious consequences were felt by certain members of the command later on because representatives of the civilian authorities were voicing an opinion that individuals had imposed their will through this report, and Simo Zaric was particularly targeted, as he was a commander -- Assistant Commander for Morale, who was, one could say, was the author of this report, the main author. And from then on certain pressures were brought to bear on the command for Simo Zaric to be sidelined, and me as well, as well as other members of the command who had expressed their satisfaction. But all of us had in fact expressed our dissatisfaction with this state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was Simo Zaric allowed to speak at that meeting, to take the floor, when the report was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not. At that meeting virtually no command members spoke, except the commander himself, who said a few words. But the very active participants were members of the civilian authorities who were criticising us for what we had done and reproaching us for this. So Simo himself didn't take the floor. He didn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened after that to Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Eventually, after a certain period of time, Simo Zaric was removed from his position of Assistant Commander for Morale, Religious and Legal Affairs, and he went back to the unit as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what about you? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: After a certain period of time -- and as we're talking about me, already in July 1993, up until then I was in the command, but in July 1993 upon the insistence of corps command members I asked to be transferred, and I joined the engineers regiment as Assistant Commander for Logistics there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tubakovic. I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, my name is David Re. I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The evidence you've just given, you told us about a meeting. It was after the civilian authorities came to learn of the report. Was the meeting called to discuss the contents of the report?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was, to discuss the content of the report. Exactly. That was exactly the topic of the meeting. The meeting -- at the meeting, the command and the civilian authorities discussed about what we had put in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who called the meeting? Was it the military authorities -- I'm sorry, the Posavina Brigade command, or was it the civilian authorities who called the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting -- the only ones who can call a meeting of the command -- the meeting was called by the command and of the brigade probably -- not probably but certainly at the insistence of representatives of the civilian authorities because they insisted that this subject should be discussed. We in the command had been discussing this at several meetings before that and thoroughly prior to the adoption of that report and we adopted it as our report. However, it reached them, and after that we had that meeting held with representatives of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Can I just ask you in answering the question to answer it as briefly as you can, and just -- just the short question I'm asking. It will be much quicker for all of us if we do it that way. Where was the meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The meeting was held at Pelagicevo in the village where the brigade command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who from the civilian authority -- sorry, which civilian officials were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic, the President of the Municipality; Milan Simic, the President of the Executive Board; Stevan Todorovic, the head of the Public Security Station; a certain person by the surname of Ninic, whose first name I do not know; and at this point I cannot recall the others but these three were there certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you remember whether Miroslav Tadic was there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think that he wasn't. I don't think that he was present. No, no, he certainly was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Bozo Ninkovic and Mirko Lukic, Simeon Simic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Bozo, Mirko, Simeon Simic were there certainly. Now you've jogged my memory. Simeon Simic was there certainly, and Bozo Ninkovic as well, and Mirko Lukic also. They were there. Yes, in addition to the people whom I have already enumerated, these were persons were also there certainly but Miroslav Tadic was not there to the best of my recollection. I don't think that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a number of civilian officials spoke at the meeting. Did Blagoje Simic speak at the meeting? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The civilian authorities I think you said had all read the report and were all very familiar with what you'd written; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were familiar with the content of the report. I don't know how they had arrived at it and how they had gotten hold of it. I suppose that the commander had given it to them. Because the position of the command was that the report should be filed and should be for the sole use of the command in seeking to overcome these problems and that it should not reach the civilian authorities because it did deal with the problems affecting civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's dated the 1st of December, 1992. When was the meeting in relation to the publication of the report? How soon afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: After a couple of days. It was towards the end of November. I believe it was the 28th or the 29th of November that the report was adopted, and this meeting was held right away, at the beginning of December, quite quickly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your evidence I think you said that the document was discussed in some detail. What did Blagoje Simic say to the meeting about the -- about the report?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't only Blagoje. All of them sought -- tried to negate what we had highlighted as negative practices, negative trends within the zone of responsibility of the brigade, i.e. the civilian organs. They tried to do that. They were even reproaching us because they said if we were to write about the situation in this territory it was a matter for the civilian authorities and not for the military authorities to draw up such reports and that it was the essence of all their statements at that meeting. Of course, I cannot recall all the details, but I do remember that some said, "You don't know what you're doing. You are doing something which -- you are way out of line. This is beyond your competence."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to concentrate for a moment on Blagoje Simic. What do you remember him saying at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably something along the lines of what the other people were saying, that he didn't agree to us having done that. I cannot remember details. I know that they were displeased at what we had written. Him in particular, and also Stevan Todorovic, they were -- because they held key positions in civilian authorities, the most responsible posts at that time. At this moment I cannot remember the details really.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was their concern the fact that the military had written this report about what the civilians were doing rather than it was what the civilians were doing? I'm saying was their concern the fact that you, the military, had written this? Do you follow what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, exactly. That was it precisely. We gained the impression that they resented the fact that it was us analysing the situation in this area, the situation among the population. They said, "It is up to you. Yours is to take care of the army, of the military issues, and it is up to us to see to what is happening amongst the civilian population." That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is were they disputing the contents of it or disputing the fact that you had written the report? Was there anger with the fact that you wrote it or that you were saying these things?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: They were angry, rather, because we had drawn up the report, because of that fact. The negative tendencies which were in evidence were something that was not to be actually referred to, and we had put that on paper, and that was what had irritated them. Do you understand me? They resented the fact -- they were angry because we had highlighted these facts, that there had been looting, that there had been crimes which had been committed by people who were not within the army and which was not within the competence of the army but was within the territory of the zone of the responsibility of our brigade. And this is what they resented and that is what upset them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That these crimes were being committed by people who were under the control of the civilian authorities, that is, the Crisis Staff, War Presidency; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- precisely that. It was out of the competencies of the terms of reference of the activities of the command of the brigade, and this is what they resented. They were angry because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But the Crisis Staff or the civilian officials there didn't in that meeting deny any of the allegations which you had made in the report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: They did not negate it. They did not deny it. They couldn't. These were certain facts which could not be denied, but they were simply angry because it had been the brigade command that had undertaken that analysis, and that was the basis reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said in your evidence earlier that Simo Zaric was particularly targeted in that meeting. Who do you remember particularly targeting him in the meeting? Who was the -- who was the person or people who were saying the things against Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was Stevan Todorovic primarily, as the head of the Public Security Station. He spoke against Simo Zaric. And also the others did. They didn't have anything personally against Simo. That's not what I said. But they immediately expressed their position to the effect that it had been Simo's doing, that the author was Simo, because in the final analysis he did actually draw up or shape the final report. It could not have been written by all the members of the command. They had all their individual inputs into the making of that report, but he was the one who finally shaped it and that is why he -- they targeted him more. They said that it was a tendentious report, that there were some unsettled pre-war accounts that were also in play there and there was some similar stories, but mainly they criticised him on account of his drawing up the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also said that Simo Zaric was removed from his position. Was that because of the influence of these civilian authorities, that is, the Crisis Staff, War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly was because of that. I'm now going to recount for you a detail, something which has given me some food for thought. For instance, Simo Zaric was a member of the command and he was in a mixed marriage. And after he had been replaced from that position, with the basic reason -- the formal reason being, you know, his wife is of another ethnicity, so if that was indeed the reason -- he could not be an assistant commander having such mixed marriage. But we also had other people holding such important positions who were in mixed marriages. So what I am trying to say is that that was precisely the reason, the actual reason being for him to be replaced from the brigade, and that was the pressures exerted by the civilian authorities. There were pressures to that effect on the commander. And formally they invoked this other being, of his being in a mixed marriage, but the actual reason was this one. The true reason was that Simo -- Simo actually was replaced from the command because he was the one who contributed the most to the drawing up of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What role did the civilian authorities, that is, the Crisis Staff, War Presidency, have in your own transfer to a different position?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: They actually wanted me to leave. It was their desire. I could feel it. And that is why of my own initiative through the corps command I requested to be replaced and to leave, because I actually could feel that this is something that they wanted. So feeling the situation, I asked them in the corps -- I told them it makes no difference to me whether I will be working here or there. So I asked them to let me leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The military and the civilian authorities, that is, Crisis Staff, War Presidency, had to coordinate certain activities in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. What sort of activities did the military and civilian authorities have to coordinate together?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: When it came to the securing of the material resources for the brigade, we relied on the command of the corps but also on the civilian authorities, for the food and the accommodation, lodgings, and other material, resources required for the army. Whereas, the control and command system in the army was wholly separated. It didn't have any formal and legal connections with the civilian authorities. The control and command system was, of course, from the command of the brigade up to the command of the corps and the main staff, but the civilian authorities could exert an influence on the army via the commander because he succumbed to such ... [End of Recording] because formally they were not entitled to interfere in what were the terms of reference of the brigade command. So in the material sense, in the provisioning sense, we did rely on them to make provisions for the army but not in this other respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was one of the reasons why the brigade command prepared and signed this document because of excessive civilian involvement in military matters?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. From May, the end of May, the 20th of May, until sometime in the end of August - that's two and a half or three months - three commanders were -- of the brigade were changed. It was precisely the civilian authorities, again thanks to their influence on the corps command, that brought about these changes. It was not the command of the corps that asked for its commander to be replaced every month. It was probably on account of their influence, the influence of the civilian authorities and of individuals within the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Blagoje Simic one of these individuals who was responsible for influencing the replacement of the three commanders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably. He probably was, because he held the most responsible position in the municipality in terms of civilian authorities. As the President of this War Presidency, i.e. of the municipal assembly, together with the President of the Executive Board and together with the head of the Public Security Station, these were the three most responsible posts as far as civilian structures of the authority were concerned. They were not your regular operations officers or anything of the kind, but they were people holding responsible posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The document you signed makes it clear that the brigade command had very, very serious concerns about what the civilian authorities were doing, such as in relation to prisoners, isolation of people, arbitrary arrests, and looting and so on. That's correct, isn't it; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It appears from the document that it was apparent to the military command of the Posavina Brigade that the civilian authorities were discriminating against people on ethnic grounds. Was that something that concerned the military command of the Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely why we had stressed these tendencies as practices which should not happen, and that is why we expressed our dissatisfaction at such -- with such practices.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's because the Posavina 2nd Brigade command was concerned that the civilian authorities - that's the Crisis Staff, War Presidency - were ordering the detention of Muslims and Croats for ethnic reasons only.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We could not justify anyone being detained without any reason, without grounds, being detained or being mistreated, and we criticised such practices as something which shouldn't happen; the command of the brigade did, that is. That is why we wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But similarly the brigade command had become aware that the Crisis Staff or War Presidency had ordered the isolation or separation of Croats, and that was something that concerned you as professional military people, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As indeed the organised looting of non-Serb -- sorry, of non-Serb properties ordered by the Crisis Staff and War Presidency. That was something that really concerned the brigade command, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The brigade command was also aware that the people who had been detained were being beaten and in some cases tortured by guards controlled by the civilian authorities, that is, the War Presidency, Crisis Staff, and the police.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had heard stories about this and people knew that this was being done and we were against it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were also aware that people had been murdered in the custody of those under the control of the Crisis Staff, War Presidency police and that was something that also seriously concerned you as professional military officers, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Re, your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Tubakovic. PRESIDING OFFICER: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No re-examination. Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Tubakovic. You can go now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: We'll have a ten-minute break. --- Break taken at 9.56 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good morning Mr. Culapovic. Could you please stand, thank you, and read the text in front of you, take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. You may sit. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Culapovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Defence of Mr. Simo Zaric, I will be conducting the examination-in-chief. I will try to go over our topics as quickly as possible. I would just like to ask you to wait for a few seconds before giving your answer after hearing my question so that we do not overlap. Let us first go through your personal details. I'll try to cover this as quickly as possible. Give us, please, first your full first name and last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Milos Culapovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you now something concerning your personal data. You were born on the 6th of May, 1948 in the village of Crkvina in Samac municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is where you have your house, in the village of Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your ancestors have been living there for generations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You're married, you have two children of age, a son and a daughter?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. My son is married, and I have a grandson; and my daughter is married as well, and I have a granddaughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You completed your elementary school in the village of Crkvina and then following that you went to school in Bosanski Samac. You are a qualified electrician by profession. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me, please, when did you leave your town and go to live abroad?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: In the second half of 1989 I went to live in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And this is where you resided permanently, worked?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I lived there on my own without my family. My family remained in Crkvina upon my departure for Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you now something about the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992. Where were you then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: In Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, please tell me, when did you come to Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I came, I believe, on the 19th of April, 1992, immediately following the breakout of hostilities in Samac because my entire family was in Samac or, rather, in Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So sometime around the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, around the 19th. We would normally come for the weekend. I think it was probably Friday or Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the main reason of your arrival?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my entire family was at home, my wife, my son, daughter, my mother, my brothers, and I was on my own in Switzerland, and it was naturally that upon the breakout of war I felt that I should be with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's understandable. So you arrived in Crkvina. And tell me, what happened afterwards? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. It took me longer to get home, longer than on previous occasions because on that occasion I came via Hungary because we couldn't travel through Croatia. I came through Hungary, through Novi Sad, to Bosanski Samac. When I got home I saw that my son had already been in the army, mobilised, and I went straight home to see my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that your son had already been mobilised, was in the army. When did your son serve his military service?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Two months prior to the breakout of hostilities my son had completed his military service in Pristina, in Kosovo, and while he was doing his military service there, the situation was very, very difficult. And mostly as a result of that I came home right away because the situation once again was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What unit was your son in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: He was in Crkvina, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. So he was in Crkvina. Now, tell me, please, where did you go following that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I took a rest, and then I went to the army command which was in the old school building where I attended my elementary school, where I started first grade. It is not far from the house of my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, who did you meet there, what transpired there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: When I got there and entered the building, I saw that there was Marko Tubakovic there. He was commander. I remember very well that there were bunk-beds there and he was on the upper bed as I entered the school building. I greeted him. And when I came there, I brought some small gifts with me, cigarettes, lighters, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps join the army? Were you yourself mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never mobilised, but at that moment when I entered we had a drink, we had a juice, and then since I had some gifts and my son was already there, they found in a wooden trunk a uniform -- or rather, it was just the jacket, the shirt of a uniform and pants. They were blue. It was a military uniform but it was very similar to the police uniform. It didn't have a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we could just slow down a little bit. So you were given a uniform. Did they tell you why you needed one?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Since I had promised that I would come again and bring some gifts with me when I come next time, they told me that I should put on the uniform as it was not advisable for a civilian to come and go into the building. It was not advisable for a civilian to move about the troops wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me please, the other soldiers that you saw there, what kind of uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: All of them had military uniforms, the old ones, the kind I wore when I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to turn now to the following day. Did you go to the town of Samac on the following day? If so, why, what was the reason, and what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I went on the following day into town because I had come from abroad and I had an obligation to acquire a permit from the Public Security Station in order to go outside of the territory of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as to the rules governing these permits, what were the rules that pertained to civilians and the rules that pertained to soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that no person could leave the town without the permit issued by the Public Security Station. As I was a civilian, I had to obtain a permit before leaving town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you came to Samac, you went to the Public Security Station. Can you tell us what went on there. Did you come across somebody there while trying to obtain a permit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I was standing in front of the station on the road, in front of it, and I was waiting for my turn to go in because I needed to wait for my turn, and there was a Zastava vehicle parked near the entrance door. It was a police vehicle. And I had put on the uniform I was given at the school from Marko Tubakovic, from our command, so I had that uniform on me. And at one point in time Savo Cancarevic, police commander, came out together with a dark-haired man that I didn't know at the time. So they came out through the entrance door and they stood in front of it and they were talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did they address you? Did you know Savo Cancarevic from before?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Savo Cancarevic is a relative of mine. I was across the road, standing by a shop selling spare parts for cars. So I was standing by that window across the road and he saw me and greeted me. And after a brief period of time, he asked me to join them. I greeted him. He asked me when I had arrived. And then he introduced me to this other man and said, "This is Crni." And this Crni, this dark-haired man, wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did anything else transpire there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Then Savo Cancarevic said that I should go to Simo Zaric to inform him and say that he needed to come to the station. I went to school with Simo Zaric, and Savo knew that I was very well acquainted with Simo Zaric and he asked me to go and inform Simo that he needed to come to the station. I asked him, "Where should I go?" And he told me, "You should go to the plum orchard, which is where the command of the 4th Detachment is located." That was the first time I had heard of the 4th Detachment. And he told me, "Here is the car. It's parked right there. Here's the key to the car and go there." So I went there and I informed Simo --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. So you came to the plum orchard to the 4th Detachment command, you saw Simo Zaric, and what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Simo. I saw a soldier and I told him I was looking for Simo. I asked the soldier where Simo was and I told him to tell him that he was sought at the police station. He called Simo and told him that Savo and Crni wanted him at the police station, and I returned with the car and left it in front of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. We should make a pause and we should slow down for the interpreters to complete interpretation. So you returned to the police station, you returned the car keys. Did you obtain your permit? How long did you stay there? And whom did you see there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed on there for another 20 minutes or 30 minutes. In the meantime, Simo arrived with another car -- or rather, he was driven there by his -- by the driver. And I saw him as he entered the Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you see what was going on inside, what was going on with Simo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Simo went upstairs. I don't know to which office exactly. I just was able to see through the large glass entrance door of the police station. I could see through a similar door into the back yard and I could see that there were police members wearing camouflage uniforms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know what Simo did there, upon getting there? You didn't see what was going on with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I think that Simo went upstairs to see somebody, perhaps Savo or somebody else upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, tell me please, did you obtain your permit to leave town?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I requested that permit. I needed to go to Belgrade as my mother was in Belgrade staying with my sister. I have a sister in Belgrade or, rather, in Batajnica, and I needed the permit in order to leave town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm now interested in this trip of yours to Belgrade. When did you go? Where did you stay? Did you meet somebody there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: The following day or perhaps that same day - I can't remember - but once I got there, one of the first persons I met there was my longtime friend Nikola Luic. Everybody who was not active in the military, who was not serving in the military, who had left earlier - and there were many of them - were in Belgrade, in downtown Belgrade, so that I saw quite a few of people from Samac in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you met Nikola Luic. Did you talk with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met Nikola Luic. We met right away, at Moskva Cafe [phoen]. We had a drink there. I told him that I had come from home, and I -- he asked me what the situation was, and I told him that there was shooting going on, that there were all kinds of things going on. I described what was happening there. And then he told me he had this idea - I don't know how it developed in his mind - but he said that he knew a journalist from Novi Sad whose name was Minja and that he could send this journalist to Samac in order to make a programme or write something for the papers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you respond to this proposal of his?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I told him that it would be best -- well, prior to that he told me that he knew Blagoje, that he knew Steve Todorovic. I personally did not know Steve Todorovic, although I did know Blagoje because he was from a neighbouring village. But I told him that he should speak to them on the phone and tell them about this, tell them that he knew this journalist who could write a story or perhaps record a TV programme, but I just simply couldn't decide on this on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And following that, did you return to Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I returned to Samac and I forgot about this conversation. I spent some time with Nikola in Belgrade. We talked about other things. But as far as this interview -- potential interview is concerned, we didn't elaborate that any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So after that you returned to Samac, and did something else happen regarding that conversation you had with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I almost forgot about that conversation. But the following day they called me on the phone - I was at home - and Savo Cancarevic was on the phone telling me that Steve needed me to come to the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you go to the station?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I didn't know what was it all about, but it was a bit of an uncomfortable situation for me. And as I got to the station, he told me that he had talked to Nikola Luic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Who said so?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Steve. Steve asked me to come to his office upstairs and told me that he had spoken to Nikola on the phone and that Nikola had said that he would ensure that the journalist would come and that I would need to go and fetch the journalist as the journalist was from Novi Sad. Nikola would ensure that he would come to Belgrade, and then I was supposed to go to Belgrade and get him there. And this is when I learned why is it that he had called me to come to the station and I was a bit more at ease after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did they provide transportation for you? Did they give you all of the documents you needed in order to leave town? Did they give you any documents for the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they gave me travel orders and they gave me a Golf vehicle. And either that same day or the following day I went to Belgrade, I got in touch with Nikola, and in the meantime Nikola had brought the journalist to Belgrade. I don't know whether the journalist came to Belgrade on his own or whether Nikola went there to fetch him. I don't know. I didn't ask about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say Minja, you mean this journalist?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard later on that his name was Milan or Milovan, so it was Minja for short. I think his surname is Pavlovic, if I'm not mistaken. I think that was his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you saw your friend Luic, and there you found the journalist Minja. Was anyone else with him there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a cameraman with a camera. And again, we met at Terazija Street [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take them to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We headed off towards Samac along the route Bijeljina-Brcko-Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During your trip, were there any conversations amongst you as to what they were interested in, what they wanted to film over there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I didn't enquire much. They asked me where I came from. I said I was from Samac or, rather, from Crkvina. En route we came across several military checkpoints who -- and they checked our papers. And as we saw soldiers en route - and this was new for me too - he asked me where the main command of that army was. I didn't know exactly whether it was in Brcko or Pelagicevo. I hadn't spent enough time to learn all these things, though I was interested of course too, because my brothers and son were in the army and this is a small town. So the discussion was whether it was in Brcko or Pelagicevo. And as we got to a checkpoint outside Brcko, I asked one of the soldiers at the checkpoint where the command was and he told me that it was in Pelagicevo. Since Minja, after that -- I didn't know why he was asking me that. Then he asked me where Pelagicevo was. I told him it was on the road to Samac, it is at the crossroads at Loncari. You take a turning, and then it's 2 or 3 kilometres away. And as I was from the area, I knew this. And then he said could we drop in at the command headquarters? And I said, "Why not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you arrived at Pelagicevo. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: There were two soldiers at the gate. It's a private house, it's a small village. I didn't really know where it was. And they told us, "Turn left. It's 50 metres on the right-hand side." And you could see some military vehicles there, so we recognised it. And then this journalist got off. He had this card of his as a journalist. He had it on his pocket, and he said that he was a journalist from Novi Sad, could he speak to the commander-in-chief. And then one of the soldiers went inside. I was sitting in the car in the immediate vicinity and I was able to watch. After a very short time the soldier returned and invited the journalist to go inside. After that, the cameraman was called in as well and he, too, left, so I assumed that they would be preparing a programme, an interview or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't go inside.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Because when I went to Belgrade, I was in civilian clothes and it wasn't suitable. But I didn't even try. They probably would not have allowed me in anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me roughly how much time they spent inside?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: It's rather hard to tell after such a long time, but roughly I would say about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And after they came out, tell me, where did you go there and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: We went on towards Samac, and shortly we arrived in front of the Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So when you got to the station, did you go inside, did they go inside? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, I stopped in front of the Public Security Station on the left-hand side of the road. They got off. I remember very well Steve came out because the policeman on duty was outside and I told him to tell somebody upstairs that the journalist had arrived. So Steve came out, he welcomed him, and they went inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I left the car and went home, though Steve said he would take care of everything and he would call me when they needed to go back to Belgrade, for me to take them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me what happened that day, the next day. When did you meet the journalists again?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: They spent that day in Samac. How their stay was organised, I don't know, because I wasn't there. However, the next day in the morning I was called again that I needed to drive them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you agree to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because talking to this Pavlovic, en route we go to know each other better as we travelled together and I felt it was my duty to drive him back to Belgrade, to Lulic [phoen]. And after that, whether he would take him back or he would go back on his own to Novi Sad, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you got to Samac. And where did you find the journalists again?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Again in front of the Public Security Station. They were outside, both the journalist and the cameraman holding the camera. They got into the car, and we were ready to go. Actually, as I was coming to the station, across the road from it they were coming out of the yard, across the way from the Public Security Station, where there are two private houses when you go inside this passageway, and they were coming out of that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you all met there in front of the Public Security Station, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they got into the car, and we set off towards town because as we were leaving, Minja asked me could we pass through the main road for him to film the town a little because it was his first visit to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. Why not? So I went along the main street, the high street, and then we made a turn to go to Belgrade, and the cameraman filmed a couple of buildings, the streets, and so on. That was all that I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And then after that I assume you set off for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the way back we didn't stop much except, I think, somewhere to have a drink or something. And in Belgrade Nikola met us. They exchanged greetings. He asked them whether they had finished their job, and we said goodbye. After that I didn't see them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after those events, how much longer did you stay in the territory of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: From the time I arrived until I went back, I stayed in all 10 to 12 days. So it was sometime at the beginning of May that I went back, because the 1st of May was a holiday, I remember that. In Switzerland too it is celebrated, so that I think I set off that day to be able to start way the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Samac, did you perhaps have occasion to see this programme that was filmed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was to be aired in a day or two, and I did watch it, but unfortunately only the beginning because the electricity went off that evening. But the next time when I came - and I came again at the end of May with a truckload of humanitarian aid that we had collected in Switzerland - I watched this programme. I took a videotape from someone who had taped it for me to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. LAZAREVIC [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Madam Presiding Officer. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Culapovic, my name is Di Fazio. I am a prosecutor. I've just got a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm at your service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you the gentleman who is also known as Culap? Is that your nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I do have the Culap nickname, but that is not my nickname only as an individual. My surname is Culapovic, so all persons, all my family members -- there are five or six men in the family, and they're all nicknamed Culap. So it's not specific to me alone, but it is the abbreviated surname and they call all of us by that abbreviated name, my brothers, my son, my brother's son, my father, and everyone. We're all known as Culap.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were all your brothers lives in Bosanski Samac during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And your first name is, of course, Milos, or Milo.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Were you a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Bosanski Samac? I know you arrived in April and you left again for the month of May. But for the rest of the year, did you stay in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of May, I went back to Switzerland, and then I came again from Switzerland between the 27th and the 29th of May with a couple of friends from Samac and with a truck loaded with humanitarian aid, hospital beds and medicines. I'm sorry, I didn't know you would be asking me this, because I have the documents which I could have brought with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... all I want to know is did you remain in Bosanski Samac throughout the remainder of that year, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever perform any guard duties at the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I haven't been issued weapons or anything. There were no -- my name was not in the records, either in the police nor in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you ever present during interviews of any prisoners in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't even know that there were any prisoners in the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As far as the organisation of this interview that you have given us, that you've told us about is concerned, the only thing that you know is that Todorovic approached you and asked you to go and collect these journalists in preparation for the interview. You don't know whose decision it was to hold these interviews. You don't know who was the prime mover behind the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I assume that the contact between Luic and Todorovic, when they spoke they decided about the journalist because Nikola told me that he knew Todorovic. MR. DI FAZIO: Madam Presiding Officer, would you just give me a moment to confer with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know of any other Milos Culapovic living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: My father's name is Milan Culapovic, but I don't think there's anyone called Milos Culapovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And he was, I assume, a fairly elderly man in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 68 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right ... [End of Recording] So you weren't present at any time in the SUP building when a woman was stripped and beaten by paramilitaries. You don't recall any such episode? You were present at no such episode?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Never. I never saw any such thing, nor was I present at any such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Osman Josarevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: There are a number of Josarevics, but Osman I don't know. I know another Josarevic, but I don't know whether his name was Osman because he was a hunter, as I was. I think his name is Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So, therefore, you weren't present on any occasion when a man named Osman Josarevic was beaten in the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Grga Zubak?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever guard him in the TO building?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. We know each other from before the war, and we were good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And do you know a place in Bosanski Samac known as the Utva factory?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever transport prisoners there so that they could have dinner -- their lunch, rather?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, never. I was working abroad. I would just come once a month, sometimes twice a month on a weekend, in no military or police capacity. I had no involvement whatsoever. And may I add, regarding those of us who were abroad, there was some scepticism towards us. I noticed this later. There was a degree of mistrust because we were abroad and at the very outset people thought now, who knows who they're connected to over there and things like that. So we didn't have much access really to these military and police organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Omer Nalic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know him well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: We were friends before the war. He's an electrical technician and I'm a highly skilled electrician, so we would work together before. But he was employed in a state-owned institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentlemen named Pasaga Tihic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We're also great friends to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Namik Suljic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, known as "the professor." He was my son's teacher, and I see him now too. I saw him two or three months ago. He is living in Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He was a policeman, I think, before the war. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sorry, Suljic, Namik Suljic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: Namik Suljic was a teacher in school. My son was his pupil. There must be a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On the day that you took these journalists and finally got them into Bosanski Samac, did you see a gentleman named Fadil Topcagic in the vicinity, in the vicinity of the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: MILOS CULAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. I've got no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No re-examination. PRESIDING OFFICER: No re-examination. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Culapovic for coming here today. You can go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: We'll have a ten-minute break. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 10.51 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good morning, Mr. Sjencic. Could you please stand and read the solemn declaration, reading the pink sheet of paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Defence for Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sjencic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you be so kind as to give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Sjencic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of March, 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born, Mr. Sjencic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I was born in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, are you married?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I am divorced.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I have a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, of what ethnicity are you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how long have your ancestors been living in Samac territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I do not have a precise answer to that question, but for at least 200 to 300 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sjencic, you completed primary school in Crkvina, the secondary economic school in Samac, and the Faculty of ... [End of Recording] Economics in Banja Luka in 1951. Sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And you served your military service near Zagreb in 1982 and 1983?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From 1975 you were a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: That of the -- of reformist forces of Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And as of the beginning of 1993, you have been a member of the SDS and you are still a member of the municipal board of that party.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sjencic, prior to the outbreak of the armed conflict in Samac municipality, you were working with the Stil factory of furniture in Samac. In fact, you were the director of that factory from 1988 to 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sjencic, there is no dispute about the fact that before the hostilities in Samac municipality break out, ethnic tensions mounted. Tell us, how did you notice this phenomenon? How did you experience it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Well, going about my regular duties, work in my regular -- at my regular workplace and living in Samac, I -- and given the political situation generally in the former Yugoslavia, the secession of the republics through war in the neighbourhoods, for instance, Croatia, and this very tense and charged inter-ethnic atmosphere was something which could also be [indiscernible] to Samac itself. There that already existed these inter-ethnic tensions. There were certain provocations also, et cetera. Simply speaking, living and working there one could feel the presence of this inter-ethnic chemically charged atmosphere, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of any roadblocks, any barricades being erected, of any guards being posted or any similar information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have some knowledge about such things. Moving around town itself, at the beginning of this year, which is to say we did it prior to the outbreak of the war hostilities, there existed barricades and I noticed two in two points in the city, the entrance to Modrica and the entrance to Orasje. And I passed by these roadblocks twice. They were manned by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sjencic, after the 17th of April, you became a regular member of the Posavina Infantry Brigade -- the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And you held this position until August 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us whether in the period from April to August you discharged any other duties as part of your work obligation, or were you just a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: In view of my education and my working experience before the war, the Ministry of -- said to me -- put me in charge of another work duty towards the end of April, I believe it was the 30th of April, 1992, and they assigned me to the post of director or coordinator of the branch office of the Doboj commercial bank. The branch office was in Samac. But this work duty did not relieve me of my military obligation, so when I was -- in those days when I was not engaged working for the army, I worked in this branch office of the Doboj commercial bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us, how did the bank function in this wartime period? Did it function normally? Did it offer the normal, regular services to its clients, to the citizens, to workers? Just explain the situation in respect of that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: This branch office, I had had also before the war -- it worked with households, which is to say dinar saving, foreign currency saving, and current accounts and other businesses connected with enterprises, the enterprise sector and the company that was done in the Doboj bank. From the time I arrived at the bank, we did work related to households and to citizens in general, which meant paying out of salaries, deposits of -- savings deposits, withdrawal of money from savings deposits and the like. For, this was -- these were the common financial transactions that this particular branch was confined to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sjencic, was the bank rendering services to all citizens of all ethnicities at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, to all ethnicities, all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in August you became Secretary of the Secretariat for the Economy of Samac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you explain how you were assigned to that post.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: It was perhaps on the 1st of August. A talk was -- the executive board members talked to me, the executive board, of course, of Samac Municipality. They invited me for a discussion, their intention being to fill the vacant post of the Secretary of the Secretariat for the Economy. And after a brief discussion with them of about half an hour, I accepted the position because it meant also relieving me of my duty as part of my military obligation. They had in mind my pre-war working experience, so they offered me this post and I accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then we can assume that it's a fact, you became a member of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do you know who held the post of Secretary for the Economy in Samac Municipality before you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
