utterances.text: I know I attended several -- I attended several meetings. It was Mr. Lazar Mirkic who after several months went to -- was assigned to another post in Samac -- in Brcko, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain to us what are the tasks in wartime, under war conditions, of the Secretariat for the Economy. What were the specific fields of work covered by the secretariat during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you see, the economic and -- which the economic agents were operating also prior to the outbreak of the war in Samac had been quite unfavourable and extremely complex, due to prophesies that had already been unfolding also outside Samac. And in view of the fact that at the time I was a director, even before the war one had to be of exceptional ability and resourcefulness in order to carry out one's work as well as properly. In view of this situation, the situation was also -- it was in such a situation that war also broke out with all the consequences which this entailed, it was very hard to manage the economic sector and to be in charge of economic exercises. What war brought by definition, which meant devastation and destruction of economic facilities, it also entailed a shortage of manpower because mostly all the able-bodied conscripts had already been recruited into the army. These were all major factors which adversely affected the operation of the economic. The market links had been severed. The roads were impassable, apart from the fact that they were unsafe. The PTT communication network was done or was severed in places. There was a severe shortage of all forms of energy, starting with electric power. There was, of course, a shortage of all sorts of fuel, primarily of oil and oil derivatives. The payment operation system did not function in the true sense of word, and all these were aggravating factors which were adversely reflected -- actually reflected the economic environment in which one was supposed to work. So the basic task of the Secretariat for the Economy and of the executive board, one can say, also was to secure, to ensure, the best possible provisions -- provisioning of the population, supplies to the population and to the army of all sorts of -- with all sorts of consumer goods, namely in addition to the discharge of certain public functions, certain public enterprises which namely supplied the citizens with water, electricity, saw to city sanitation and maintenance and cleaning. These also had to be involved, to provide such advice, and it was also our task to set in motion certain industrial and economic capacities and facilities in the city's area which was possible to set in motion. The working hours which were prescribed were up to 2.00, for these were really exceptional conditions and one needed to exert really more than average efforts in order to achieve all these tasks. This was more or less the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained the tasks of the secretariat. Would you please explain to us how did you go about organising the work of the secretariat in order to indeed implement those tasks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the organisation, we already have a sort of an organisational pattern which had been set in place prior to my assumption of that post. I had associates within the secretariat who were in charge of specific fields, and we had people who we called coordinators in charge of the public enterprises in the area. We called them "war coordinators." And we also had commissioners in the local communes in the area. So this was the general infrastructure which was to enable the functioning of the economy in the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, what was the attitude of the executive board of the municipality and the departmental ministries.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: You mean the departmental ministries in the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Well, in such a situation where government sought to pass such regulations and subsidiary legislation to regulate the field of the economy, and it was our task to abide by such regulations which were then published in the Official Gazette, and we had to execute and respect the regulations they adopted. The communication, physically speaking, telephone lines, well -- was difficult, but ministers came to visit - for instance, the agriculture minister came to visit - and there were other relevant people who came to visit us in order to further our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So we can know that you had to respect those decisions but also to implement them to the extent which was possible given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that can be noted. And it was on the basis of these decrees, also that and other regulations passed by the government, that we brought in our own conclusions, our own decisions to give them effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We should be regarding to that subject in a while. You explained that the situation was difficult, that there was no power, that there was no water, that the city came under constant shelling. You told us -- was there a certain number of refugees from other territories of Bosnia or from Croatia? Had any refugees come to Samac and were they also in your charge? Were you also in charge of resolving their problems?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. The executive board had also the task of addressing their problems because a huge number of refugees had flocked into Samac and that was something which was not -- something one could not plan. The tasks in respect of them could not be planned. There were several thousand refugees accommodated in Samac. This was a very difficult problem. It was an aggravating factor in the sense that it was a very hard problem because we needed to provide accommodation, food, and medical care, and normal living conditions -- as normal as possible living conditions with such a huge number of them. And that was one of our priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sjencic, further, a while ago that the majority of the population of the citizens from the territory of Samac were in the army. How did you manage to resolve all these formidable and numerous questions that fell within your field of competence and your area of work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: To carry out our tasks we -- given this shortage of manpower and professionally qualified personnel, we mainly had -- liaised with the Department of Defence in Samac, which had a thankless role at the time because we wanted to have as many people as possible assigned to work duty, and of course it was the aim of the army to have as many soldiers as possible, so that the Ministry of Defence was between hammer and endless work. But we managed to resolve these problems together on the basis of consultations and agreement and as far as possible in the given situation. Otherwise, economic agents, which is to say enterprises, actually got their own war duty assignments of working posts, and these were approved by the executive board. The executive board was a filter which actually concerned whether this scheme of work posts was indeed acceptable or not. Then the coordinators would ask the Ministry of Defence for a certain number of people to be assigned to work as part of the work obligation or work duty in order to fill these posts according to that particular scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sjencic, can we then agree that those people who were not on the front or were not in the military, all of them had a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether records were kept of those people who had work obligation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I believe that the Department of the Ministry of Defence had full records about people with work obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: During wartime conditions in Samac municipality and while these people were engaged in their work obligation, do you know whether they received any compensation for their work, any remuneration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, they received it. I believe that in the first few months it was difficult to organise it, but if I remember well either in August or September the remuneration or compensation for four months was paid out for people who had work obligation. Those were not high sums, but the compensation was paid out sometimes in cash and later on and much more frequently in kind. It was given to them -- it was paid out in certain goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, why was it paid out in kind rather than in cash, compensation for their work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I've already said that one of the negative factors that influenced the operation of the economy was the insufficient amounts of cash. We had rampant inflation at the time, and if you were late in picking up your salary for just one day, the following day it was devalued by some 20 to 30 per cent. So due to insufficient amounts of cash and due to inflation, we frequently opted for paying out compensation in kind because there is a shortage of foodstuffs, hygiene items and so on, so that the workers and people with work obligation accepted it and preferred that, rather than payment in cash.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that what people received in kind was in fact more valuable than payment in cash?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sjencic, you explained to us what were the duties and tasks of the Secretariat for Economy. Could you please tell us, since you were also a member of the executive board, what were the tasks of the executive board in wartime in 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I attended sessions of the executive board. In addition to organising the economy itself, which was a priority, they also had to enable to operation of the hospital. We had a haemodialysis centre, and we had to provide everything that was needed, in terms of medication and everything else for people using haemodialysis. Therefore, non-economic activities such as education, sport, culture, taking care of refugees and so on, those were the primary tasks of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please whether the executive board while trying to carry out all of these tasks and duties, did it also pass some conclusions, orders, decisions and so on? Can you explain to us the way it operated.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. The technicalities of its work. We met almost daily in view of the situation that was subject to changes, frequent changes. So we tried to adapt to that and we passed our regulations based on government decrees. We adapted to the situation in Samac, and we passed various decisions, decrees, instructions, and so on. We always attempted to formulate them and put them into writing, and that was the easier part of the job. It was much easier to do that than to implement these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, were these documents mandatory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were and some of them were not. If our regulations were of general nature, then they applied to everyone, to the entire population, to the economy of the entire municipality of Samac. Some regulations were of a selective nature, which meant that they were mandatory only for the entities to which the regulation itself pertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether any regulation, decision, instruction passed by the executive board contained any discriminatory aspect with respect to the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such decision or conclusion. And I believe that this is not how we viewed the matters. This is not how we looked at this. We tried to enable everything that was needed for normal life to go on, but we never passed such conclusions or decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Secretariat for Economy and the executive board both had quite a number of tasks, tell us please, how did people move about on the ground within the municipality and outside of Samac municipality? Were they able to move about freely, or did they need to have a permit? And if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: In view of wartime conditions, the movement of people and goods was difficult and risky as well. The people who were fixed for military service and those who were in the army, their movement outside of the municipality was subject to certain permits and passes issued by the army command. As far as the rest of the population is concerned and their movement within the municipality, they were able to move about the municipality freely. And if they needed to leave the territory of the municipality, I believe that they needed a permit issued by the police. This pertains to those who were not set for military service and who were not considered military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You, as part of your work obligation, served as Secretary for Economy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Secretariat for Economy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you need to have a permit if you wanted to leave Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I needed it. First I would receive my travel order from the executive board. Since my work obligation was also considered my wartime assignment and I was a military conscript, then pursuant to my travel orders I had to go to the army command and obtain a permit to leave the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute ago you told us that you had to comply with the decrees of the government of Republika Srpska. Are you aware of the decree passed by the government of Republika Srpska concerning the gathering and distribution of war spoils?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that decree. I believe that it was passed in June and it was a decision on collecting and distributing war spoils, and a few days later an instruction on implementation of that decree was passed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And I assume that that decree was adopted by the executive board.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: The decree itself had a mandatory nature, as far as the executive board is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the instruction on implementing the decree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Crisis Staff analysed this matter and passed a conclusion mandating the Secretariat for Economy to draft an instruction on recording and creating an inventory of the spoils of war, and we did pass an instruction of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, how were the spoils of war gathered, in what manner? Where was it warehoused? What kind of goods were there and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Certain enterprises were tasked with collecting spoils of war, and we were particularly interested in rounding up cattle as well as perishable foodstuffs. And when it came to this type of spoils of war, we had designated two locations. When it came to cattle, that was taken to the farms of the agricultural enterprise. And when it came to pigs, they were taken to farms in Zasavica, and there this was placed under the jurisdiction of the agricultural cooperative from Samac. As far as other goods are concerned, there were several other warehouses designated for those goods, state-owned company Utva, state-owned company Korpara, both in Samac, and also company Sirovinaprodukt, which had its headquarters in Doboj and branch offices in Samac. As far as the grains are concerned, those were stored in silos of the agricultural enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, then, what was the role of the republic agency for commodities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: When it came to these reserves, I told you that there was a decree of the government and the spoils of war, in fact, represented reserves, reserve commodities, and they had their headquarters -- this agency had their branch office in Samac as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Were the spoils of war collected in Odzak municipality and do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in Odzak municipality there was a problem with rounding up cattle, and agricultural cooperative Agropromet was in charge of that. This is what I know mostly concerning that. So Agropromet was in charge of that and cattle was brought to these two sites that I'd already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You haven't told us this: Pursuant to whose orders was this carried out? There was a military administration there, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a military administration in Odzak, and all of the contents went to the military administration regarding all of the activities that were carried out. And I believe that in order to do that a consent had to be obtained from the military administration because it would have been impossible to do it without that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you know about the authorities, scope of authorities, and the relations between military authorities on one hand and civilian authorities on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: The relations were clearly set out by regulations. Civilian authorities had their own realm, and the army had its own. The contacts between civilian and military authorities mostly went through the Department of Ministry of Defence. I've already told you about this, when it came to work force and so on. According to what I know, it was impossible for civilian authorities to interfere in the scope of authorities of the military. There might have been some insignificant, minor conflict because the military perhaps exerted quite -- a great deal of pressure on civilian authorities when it came to foodstuffs, fuel, and other goods that were needed by the military. And in that respect, the military insisted on things done either quicker or in greater quantities, and we were not always able to accommodate them. So that was in general the description of the relations between the military and civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So we can say that civilian authorities managed or did the best it could under wartime conditions to help the army to the best of its abilities.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could say so. PRESIDING OFFICER: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell us, what were the relations like between the executive board and the Crisis Staff? How did this function?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I did not attend sessions of the Crisis Staff. Based on my knowledge, the president of the executive board contacts said Crisis Staff when needed, and he was invited to attend Crisis Staff sessions as needed when -- he had the discretion to inform us of this when he found it necessary. If certain conclusions were passed by the Crisis Staff and they were mandatory for the executive board, we had to implement them and the reports went between the Crisis Staff and the executive board every fortnight or once a month according to the arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sjencic, please tell us whether Mr. Blagoje Simic personally -- personally issued orders to the Secretariat for Economy or you yourself.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: In his contacts with me, he occasionally wanted to know my opinion, my professional opinion. He was a politician who wanted to acquire information from a number of sources. Now, as to direct orders issued by Mr. Blagoje Simic to the Secretariat for Economy, there were none. I mentioned the conclusion that mandated for the Secretariat for Economy to collect war booty, but I don't remember any other examples. We had contacts between the Crisis Staff and the Secretariat for Economy, but they were mostly of the informal nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sjencic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: Cross-examination for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Sjencic, David Re is my name. I'm working with the Prosecution. I'm just going to ask you a few questions about the evidence you've just given us. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I'd just ask you to be -- to assist everyone, to be as brief as possible in the answers you give and listen very carefully to the questions I ask. Would you be able to assist with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, fine. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are -- you stood for the municipal assembly in October 1990 as a political candidate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that. If you mean the elections in October 1990, yes. If you're referring to the elections when I was in the Party of Reformist Forces, I was on the ticket, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were member 33, I think, on the ticket, according to the list.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly which number I was on the list, if we are talking about the list of the Party of Reformist Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The election on the 29th of October, 1990, that was the first elections -- free elections in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't remember the ordinal number under which my name appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... really important. You weren't elected, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence was that you were in the 2nd Posavina Brigade after the 17th of April, 1992. Which military detachment were you attached to before the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: That military detachment was called the 4th Detachment. That's how we called it in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were a member of the 4th Detachment on the 17th of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your duties as a member of the 4th Detachment on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I was an ordinary soldier in the 4th Detachment. I wasn't aware that the war had started. I was in my apartment on the 17th of April and early in the morning I heard shooting in town. I didn't have any specific duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you -- when were you called up to go and fight?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of April in the morning, with some effort I left Samac and went to Crkvina because a friend of mine had asked me to take his parents and wife to stay with my parents, believing that it would be safer for them there. I stayed in Crkvina, I can't remember exactly, two or three days, endeavouring together with the military commanders to cross into the battalion of Crkvina, the Crkvina Battalion, because that is where my family was and my friends and so on. As the army did not allow it, I was not successful. I returned to Samac into the SIT state-owned company, and I was assigned to I don't remember which company.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... all I was asking was when. Do you remember a moment ago I was asking if you could be as brief as possible. The question was: When? Could you just give us a date, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: It could have been the 19th of April, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, you were appointed Secretary of the Secretariat of Economic Affairs. Were you a member of the SDS at the time you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The structure you gave us a moment ago I think was as the Secretary of the Secretariat of Economic Affairs you reported to the president of the executive board. Is that right; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that Mirko Lukic at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: No. It was Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, followed by Mirko Lukic. I'm sorry, it was my mistake. Milan Simic reported, of course, to the Crisis Staff or War Presidency from where he obtained his directions; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He received directions from them, and we also had decrees of the government of Republika Srpska. But he was the person that contacted the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because the Crisis Staff and War Presidency at that time were performing all the duties normally undertaken by the municipal assembly. That was the time ... [End of Recording].

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff and the War Presidency was a body that replaced the assembly up to the moment when the assembly itself was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff and War Presidency in turn reported back, taking its orders from the government of Republika Srpska, that is, the prime minister, presidency, and the Serbian assembly, the National Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever was binding for the civilian authorities, that was covered by regulations and that is how this functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And each of the bodies, that is, Crisis Staff, War Presidency, executive board, and your own position as the Secretary of the Secretariat of Economic Affairs, you -- each of these had to implement government decrees, policies, and laws, including those of the national assembly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: All the regulations and laws that were officially published in Official Gazettes were for me and the executive board binding to the extent that we were able to implement them under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence earlier was of the terrible economic conditions in Samac at the time. You talked about inflation. You talked about basically the collapse of the local economy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you told us that -- in effect that money was worthless and you were paying people -- or people were being paid in kind because they couldn't buy anything with the worthless currency because of the high inflation or could buy very little with the money.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. And money lost value very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in those times a barter economy developed, didn't it? People were trading in whatever valuable goods they could get their hands on because the money was not worth anything.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: There were certain compensatory arrangements between state-owned companies. There was some degree of normal payments where this was accepted by agreement. So there were some normal relations. The market in those days was the market of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The payment system was not functioning between these two states so that we mostly had these barter deals between the two. And within Republika Srpska there were some payments through giro accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At a more personal level, a local level, the citizens of Samac were bartering between themselves because of the worthlessness of the currency, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: We tried to supply the population with all types of consumer goods, foodstuffs and so on. And they were able to purchase those goods with currency. But individual barter exchanges between inhabitants, I can't remember. I don't know about that. I don't know whether someone may have given someone a packet of cigarettes for a bottle of oil, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But certainly hard currency was more valuable than the local currency, the Deutschmark, the US dollar; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And quite natural for people to want to get their hands on hard currency if they possibly could in those wartime circumstances.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: People who were fortunate enough to have hard currency, Deutschmark, US dollars, wouldn't put it in the bank, would they? They'd keep it in their house or keep it somewhere else. They wouldn't put it in the bank, would they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: They would prefer to keep it at home because of the general insecurity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: During the time of war, you had a very important position, would it be fair to say, running the economy and responsible for the running of the economy in the Samac region?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was wartime and it was very important to coordinate your economic activities with all levels, all functions of government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was important for as many entities in the economy to function as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course you coordinated your local economic activities and planning with the defence because a war -- with the Department of Defence because you were in a war situation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: With the Department of the Defence Ministry in Samac, yes, regarding the manpower itself, because through them we could obtain personnel who were engaged in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There were a lot of tasks that needed doing during the war on a local level when the men were -- men were off at the front line fighting, weren't there, because there was a severe manpower shortage in Samac during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a shortage of manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The people who had gone to war -- or the people who had been drafted into the VRS were Serbs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Mostly Serbs, but there were Croats and Muslims as well but of lesser numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time was in the area in which you were living with -- between Serbs and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, between Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But in other areas of Bosnia and the Republika Srpska the war was between Serb against combined Croat and Muslim forces, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I am not sufficiently familiar with that. There were conflicts of all kinds, but I don't know where what kind of conflicts broke out in various areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I can't give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We'll just concentrate on the local area, then. The Muslims and Croats, as you know, didn't want to be drafted into the VRS to fight against their own forces, or forces of their own ethnicity, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Most of them adopted such a position, yes. There were some who were members of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was a very, very small minority in your experience, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: One could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which left you with really only Muslims and Croats who were available to do most of the work obligation in Samac when the Serb men were off in the army fighting the war.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: There was a number of male Serbs, like myself, who were under the work obligation. A large number of Serbs were also under work obligation who were not fit for military service, so that in all local communes both men who were not fit for military service and women were engaged to carry out certain tasks in all the local communes of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The great bulk of people who were available to you for work obligation for labour were Muslim and Croat men, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: There were quite a number under work obligation, and we took into consideration what their qualifications were, and we ensigned them to companies, depending on those qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I ask you again please to listen to the question I'm asking you and concentrate on what I'm asking you. I was asking you about the great bulk of men for labour work. The great number of men available for labour work for work obligation were Muslims and Croats, weren't they? Because the Serb men who were able-bodied were off fighting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the Secretariat of Economic Affairs coordinated with the Ministry of Defence the work obligation for these men who weren't at the front line.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Only in certain situations. The managers of companies or enterprises would request from the ministry department a certain number of workers. And if a situation arose that that number did not correspond to the needs of the managers, then the Secretariat of the Economy would judge which had priority, would it be the bakery manufacturing bread, to secure the water supply system, or the loading of goods for instance. So that is when we had to join in and set the priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just go back to the question I was asking you. The Ministry of Defence had work it needed done that it couldn't use soldiers to do, and your secretariat had work which you needed to have performed which you had men to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat once again the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. I'll rephrase it for you. There were some tasks that the Ministry of Defence required people doing their work obligation to perform, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: You mean the army, the military?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And as the Secretary of the Secretariat of Economic Affairs there were things which you needed done in the municipality which you organised people to do.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: It wasn't up to me as the Secretary of the Economy to do this, but they were needed by the economy, by certain companies in the company. And the managers of those companies would submit their requests regarding a certain number of people that they needed to the Department of the Defence Ministry for manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But it was coordinated so that the Ministry of Defence could use some and the civil authorities, the companies, could use other men, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: What was left over, those that were available, they could be used by the managers of all the companies that were still functioning in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, for the record, because my learned friend mentioned civilian authorities and companies, which is ambiguous term and this witness just gave the answer -- a positive answer. But I believe that he's -- he was misled by this question since there are two terms in question, "civilian authorities" and "companies." So maybe that should be clarified now; otherwise, I'll leave it for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I have time out for the length of that objection, Madam Presiding Officer? It could have been done in three words. PRESIDING OFFICER: Are you going to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can clarify it. PRESIDING OFFICER: One minute more then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The civilian authorities needed people to clean the streets, didn't they? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: For the cleaning of streets, there was a state-owned company called Komunalac, and this company needed those men, and the coordinate -- or rather, the director of that company would request a certain number of workers for their daily activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But who would they request that from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: From the defence ministry department.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If windows needed repairing in the town or the municipality, how would that be organised?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Somebody who was responsible for that particular activity and whose task it was to repair the windows would address himself to the department. If it was in the local commune, then the commissioner for that commune could make the request for a certain number of workers. Or if it was a company, then the manager of that company would request so many workers, and then that request would be met or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who organised the civilian workers to perform trench digging at the front lines?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: We have spoken about that. The defence ministry department would assign a certain number of workers to do their work obligation in the army, and then taking care of them, driving them where necessary, feeding them, accommodating them, all that was within the terms of reference I assume of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were aware at the time when you were doing your job that the army was using civilians to dig trenches at the front line, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: The army wasn't just digging trenches. I know that they were using civilians for various needs they had, and they were several in kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Remember right at the beginning I asked you if you'd help by answering the question I asked, and you said you would? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question was: You were aware at the time, weren't you, that the army was using civilians to dig trenches at the front line?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you find this out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I know that the army was using civilians for certain tasks in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you gave evidence that you were aware the army was using civilians to dig trenches at the front line. You then said you didn't know at the time. My question was: When did you find out? That's all. When did you find out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly when I found out, but the digging of trenches was probably one of the tasks that those men were assigned. I'm telling you that they were doing other things as well and that this was within the competence of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please confine yourself to the question which I'm asking you, please, not long explanations about other things. PRESIDING OFFICER: That should be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand I have 14 minutes left over from this morning, Madam Presiding Officer. PRESIDING OFFICER: Fourteen minutes from this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weiner was keeping very strict time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. On -- the second witness cross-examination began at 10.42 and finished at 10.53, for a total of 11 minutes, which gives us 14 minutes. We could argue over a minute and say it's 13 minutes -- approximately 13 to 14 minutes. PRESIDING OFFICER: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Non-Serbs were being used to loot Serb property -- sorry, non-Serbs were being used to loot non-Serb property, that of the property of Muslims and Croats. People who were performing their work obligation were being used to loot the homes and property of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who organised that? Was it the Ministry of Defence or your department?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection for the record. The previous answer of this witness was that he doesn't have his personal knowledge at all about that, so this next -- this question is useless. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were unaware of any reports of looting of non-Serb property during the war by those doing their work obligation? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: There was looting in the territory of the municipality, committed both by members of the army. There was looting of state-owned companies and private property, and we thought to prevent it as far as that was possible. I said in my testimony that war is a state of anarchy and that we tried to put some order into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The spoils of war of which you gave evidence earlier, cattle, foodstuff, pigs, and so on, was that from -- were those spoils of war taken from the territory, taken over by the Serb forces on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Not just from those territories but from those territories as well. So I said livestock came from the area of Odzak. It was requisitioned in Samac. Mostly from all over the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the people performing their work obligation were used to assist the army in removing these spoils of war from that zone -- from that area, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. To assist the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said earlier -- you said earlier that the army used the civilians to do a lot of different thing, including trench digging. That was one of the other things the army was using the civilians to do, wasn't it, to remove the spoils of war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The refugees -- many of the refugees who arrived in Samac were housed in the houses of non-Serbs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: They were housed in all abandoned areas, all abandoned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: After the Serb takeover on the 17th of April, 1992, hundreds of Croats and Muslims were rounded up, arrested, and detained in various locations in Samac, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I have some knowledge about it, what I had heard from others, that a certain number of people were arrested and held in detention, those that were in possession of weapons unlawfully. So I do have some knowledge about it. This happened at the time when I was in the army, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The houses or flats of the people who were in detention were used to accommodate Serb refugees, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it's quite possible. I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was on the Crisis Staff in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the composition of the Crisis Staff. I know that the president of the executive board attended meetings when it was necessary. I know that Dr. Blagoje Simic was the president, and I know of a few other people, but I never read out the official composition of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Bozo Ninkovic on the Crisis Staff; yes, no, or don't know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I think he was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Simeon Simic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I assume he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Milos Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Excuse me for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, one of the decrees or policies that you followed or you had to implement was the decision on the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina of the national assembly of May 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nothing further. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sjencic, would you be kind enough and tell us of what ethnicity were the soldiers in the 4th Detachment and later of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: In the 4th Detachment there were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And later on in the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: In the 2nd Posavina Brigade, there were also members of Muslim and Croat and Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please listen carefully. In the territory of the entire Samac municipality how many people were under work obligation? Were more Serbs or more non-Serbs covered by work obligation, meaning both men and women?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I think there were far more Serbs in the territory of the whole municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: A brief question now. The Prosecutor asked you about looting and whether you knew anything about it. My question to you: Was there any organised looting by the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: No, there was organised struggle against looting by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I place on record my objection to the last question on the basis of leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What are you aware of? Did the civilian authorities order any kind of looting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge whatsoever of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination you were asked about refugees. So tell us, were there Serb refugees who came to Samac, were they accommodated in Serb villages as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question and my last one: The citizens of Samac or any other places in Samac territory whose houses were damaged by shelling, were they provided other accommodation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And of what ethnicity were the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SJENCIC
utterances.text: Of both Croat and Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Sjencic. Thank you for coming and giving your deposition today. You can go now. We'll have a one hour 15 lunch break, so we'll start again at 13.40.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good afternoon, Mr. Dujkovic. Could you please stand and read the text on the pink sheet of paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: The Defence for Mr. Simic, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dujkovic.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Please give us your full name -- your full name.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Stanko Dujkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Crkvina near Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of November, 1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Where are you living now?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am living in Bosanski Samac and I've been living there since 1977 as a permanent resident.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What is your marital status?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm married. I have one child.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And what about your ancestors? How long have they lived in the territory of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe about 200 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, you completed high school in Samac and secondary agricultural school in Derventa.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And you served your service in the JNA in Bjeleca?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From 1965 to 1966.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And you have the rank of a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the rank of a reserve major.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists until 1990, when national parties won, and since that time I no longer was a member of the League of Communists. And currently I'm not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From 1963 you were employed with the Obudovac agricultural cooperative.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, with Posavina Enterprises in Samac.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And from 1988 to 1989 in Agropromet enterprise.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And after that in the work community of the broiler cooperative?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This last post that you held in the cooperative broiler, that's where you were when the April 1992 war started?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you told me that the war had started in April 1992, tell us, what do you know about the situation which obtained then the inter-ethnic tensions? What knowledge of the situation and of such phenomena do you have?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my knowledge about the period is still fairly fresh. There are some incidents, some phenomena which are enscribed in my memory, and I should like to describe what it was that I went through at that time. In view of the fact that at the time was set up a coalition between the SDA and the HDZ parties, tensions mounted on a daily basis increasingly in Samac municipality and there were some things which were happening which only served to flare up these tensions. There was practically every night an explosion in different places outside Samac, in the periphery of the town, and this of course worried the population and I myself as a citizen of Samac was very upset. Needless to say, people were also fearful of these things. But what happened in Samac proper sometime in early autumn in 1991, namely an explosion which took place in the very centre of town in a cafe downtown which was also frequented by my son occasionally, we were all very upset, we all went out in the street. I went looking for him, and fortunately he was in another place at another cafe and not the one in which the explosion had taken place. I learned that two lads had been killed by the explosion and that a young girl of Serb ethnicity had been wounded and that two Muslim youths had been killed by the explosion. One of these lads is the son --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Mr. Dujkovic, this has been testified to on a number of occasions by other witnesses before this court. Do you have any more specific examples of the situation which obtained or other events which transpired in other places or in Samac itself?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: There are some concrete examples. For instance, I talked to this lady. She was a Serb. That was in 1991. Also, sometime towards the end of summer. We just happened to meet and we had a casual conversation on which occasion she told me that she'd heard that the -- that the priest in the village of Hrvatska Tisina after the mass addressed the present congregation and told them that Posavina should become a Croatian province and that they should move -- the Serbs should move out of Posavina. The woman who told me this story was a Croat woman. She had been in the church during the service. She was very surprised at these words. By the way, her name was Janja. And so she -- I asked her, "Where do you think we should move out, Janja?" And she said -- she said, "The priest told us that this is supposed to be a Croatian province and that you Serbs should leave, so I wonder why aren't you leaving."

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember any examples of arming?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember very well. My flat -- namely, my bedroom looks onto a cafe which was owned by a neighbour of mine who is a Muslim by the name of Osman Nesic. During this time of tense inter-ethnic relations, in contrast to the time before that, it was only Muslims dropped in his place. And one evening my wife noticed that something was being unloaded there, and quite nearby is also the building of the Serbian religious community -- sorry, of the Islamic religious community and we thought that they were unloading weapons there in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, have you any knowledge about the movement of the troops, of the armies, the HVO and other members of other Croatian units?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned about that from a friend of mine whose wife had gone to Slavonia in March -- at the end of March 1992, concretely to the village of Kopljanica because one could already feel the imminent conflict was in the air, so he moved his family to live with a friend of his who is a veterinarian just like he was. And once when he got in touch with his wife, he told me that at the football stadium in Kopljanica there were significant troops of the National Guard, the Croatian National Guard, the HVO as well, which according to his story were ready to enter Samac. I was not surprised at this; I can tell you that right away. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd like an objection to be noted on the part of the Prosecution. This evidence is, A, beyond the scope of the summary that the Prosecution has received. And secondly, it's in the Prosecution's submission quite irrelevant. So I'd like the last answer to be struck from the record and not taken into account on the basis that it's, A, outside the summary, and, B, irrelevant to the issues at trial. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Vukovic, could you just respond very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. This whole question was whether the entire context of the witness's statement, and I do not believe that it is -- goes beyond the scope of what is supposed to be the answer of the witness. But I shall leave that for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, we shall now deal with another subject. In the beginning of May 1992 you were appointed coordinator, leader, manager of the Agropromet agricultural cooperative.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was your work obligation.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you explain to us how you were appointed, by whom you were appointed, and how did this whole thing happen.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed as coordinator in the Agropromet agricultural cooperative by the Bosanski Samac Department of the Ministry of Agriculture. That was my military obligation and it was treated as such, my task being to organise production there which was ongoing. This was mostly livestock breeding, livestock production, reproduction of eggs, of broilers, and the feeding of cattle. Also, it was my obligation to provide the necessary inputs for the needs of the peasants there, of the farmers there, for them to be able to carry out the spring and autumn sowing of crops, all with a view to the provision of food to satisfy the requirements of the army and the local population ... [End of Recording] There had already been filled prior to the war and we had organised production also with subcontractors in Zasavica, with Marko Zecevic; in Hasici. I can also recall the names. Give me a minute. Bear with me for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: If you cannot remember, you can perhaps remember somebody else.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Pavo. The fattening of cattle was on the farms of Dosic Pero, Ante and Jozo Stanic, and this was mainly organised production.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So these are private farms that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are private farms and this is mainly the line of production that the cooperative engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain. How was this subject contracting, this corporation organised?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The organisation was such that the cooperative was under the obligation to provide the subcontracting farmer who owned the facility with all the inputs, the required materials, the required feed for the production, also to see to the medical care of the livestock. After the end of a shift, the facility would be emptied, the livestock would be shipped for slaughter and further processing, and the farmer in question would be paid out according to contract which was signed with him before the whole project.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us about these private subcontracting farmers from Zasavica, from Hasici whom you mentioned. Of what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during this first period, how much heads of big and large cattle did you manage to collect?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to this basic task of the cooperative and of myself who worked in it, in addition to organising production, that is, we also had to round up all the big and large cattle, "large cattle" also meaning pigs or various categories -- small cattle being pigs and the large cattle being cows, heifers, and calfs who roamed about the area without any control. So the small heads of cattle were put in Zasavica because Zasavica had facilities for the rounding up and accommodation of such cattle, and large cattle were placed in one of the plants of the agricultural industrial combine in Samac. Our task was to provide the necessary feed for that cattle, for all those animals, and also to see to their medical protest, medical care. All the cattle that had been rounded up, mainly on the large cattle which is breeding reproductive cows, with the engagement of the veterinary administration in Samac were checked and they were then handed over to the peasants to keep them and tend to them and all the others which were not capable of breeding were used for the kitchens, which were then being operational for the feeding of the population. Also the pigs in Zasavica were used for the needs of the population, that is, to feed the population and the army. All the dead cattle which was collected in the area, when we collected dead cattle and animals, we had also to disinfect the grounds and to see to it in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This means that you cooperate also with the veterinary station there.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In this period, 1992-1993, who was the chief veterinary surgeon in the veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the Serb veterinarian, there was also Hasan Izetbegovic, a Bosniak. He was a Muslim veterinarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So explain to me. So you collect these large and big and small animals and you round them up. Who was the one who made the decision whether any of the cattle could be slaughtered, shipped elsewhere for different purposes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Such decisions were made in principle by the executive board, and they were used by the army for their needs, while the kitchens which were organised in Samac were used by the SIT organisation, enterprise, for everybody, to provide food for everybody, whatever their ethnicity. And also in the church there was a kitchen that had been set up in the village of Batkusa, Obudovac, Loncari, and Pelagicevo. There had been issued an order by the executive board as to who could take any of that cattle and use it for the needs of different kitchens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that no one could take over the animals without a written permit?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, no one could. No one could actually pass through the point and take any of the meat from the slaughtered cattle because there the checkpoints at the gate to the place where the cattle were situated was manned by police. And of course they controlled whatever was taken out, exported from that particular facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "checkpoint," you also mean Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zasavica is what I had in mind because two policemen were posted there who took turns to control people coming and going, to see whether they had the permission to take meat from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, did you go to Zasavica often?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on the basis of the assignment I had, to check the condition of the livestock, whether there was a shortage of food for it, et cetera. MR. DI FAZIO: Presiding Officer, may I suggest to my colleague that we be absolutely clear about a point of the evidence raised by the witness, namely whether the two policemen who were posted at Zasavica were there solely and only to prevent people coming in and stealing meat or animals, because it's unclear from the evidence and that's a matter that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They were posted there for that particular reason because there had been attempts on theft. And I must say even from my native village there were attempts by people to go inside, to take livestock from there during the night. And that is why the policemen were posted there, to check on people coming in and going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you a moment ago whether you went to Zasavica frequently. You said you did. To the best of your recollection, what kind of population was living there, of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Croats lived there, because Zasavica was inhabited by Croats, people of Croatian ethnicity. And there were also Muslims, a certain number of Muslims from Samac itself who were stationed or moved there. They lived in a joint household with the local inhabitants or they had separate houses, as some of the inhabitants of Zasavica had already left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And was there a certain number of refugees there as well?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very soon Serb refugees arrived, and they were accommodated in the Zasavica local community, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were producing and breeding livestock and chicken at various locations. Do you know any other locations where this was done?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was another location in the territory of Odzak municipality. This is a work unit for pheasant production which was in the Merok [phoen] company of Odzak, and they manufactured pheasant chicks and they provided catering services as well. This facility, as it was under military administration in Odzak, had -- they had information that there was looting, and I was told to address a request to the command of the military administration in Odzak for that location to be freed of military administration and to be placed under the control of the cooperative Agropromet, which was able to take over this production, so that the catering establishment be repaired sufficiently to be able to provide services in accordance with its normal operations. And I received such a permission. I think it was from Colonel Pero Pasovic. That is, he signed it in response to a request addressed by me. And this pheasant farm was extracted from under the military administration. I organised repairs to the extent that it was possible and organised the production facility. About 19 people were employed there, mostly refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Dujkovic, how much was invested roughly in that pheasant farm?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I have the figures, the specific figures. 70.000 marks were invested in that facility, which once Odzak was formed again as a municipality Agropromet was never compensated for this sum by Odzak. So the food that was being manufactured there was also used to feed the army and civilians. Everything was in the service of feeding the army and the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were 19 people employed at the pheasant farm in Odzak. Tell us, please, how about the permission for movement, as it was under military administration, movement from one municipality to another?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: As this farm was extracted from under military administration only, still it was not possible to move around without permission from the military administration, so I had to provide them with a list of people who were permanently stationed at the pheasant farm, who were guarding it and working there, and of course people who would come occasionally to tour the farm I also had to ask for permission, and this applied to myself as well. If I went there, I needed to have permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, you mentioned that large and small livestock was used to feed the population and the army and you mentioned some local communities where there were public canteens. And was there such a public canteen in Samac itself?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've said that, and I'll repeat that from the very beginning of the war there was a public canteen in the SIT work organisation in Samac where in addition to the army being supplied with food the inhabitants of the town of Samac came to have their meals, those who had nothing to eat at the time, because Samac was surrounded for almost four months. It was under encirclement. And supplies for Samac could hardly reach it, so there were hardly any sources except these that I have referred to just now. This was the only source and the only method of providing for the population with food.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Among the population, who was allowed to use that canteen? People of all ethnicities, or was there any discrimination?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I myself went there often when I came back from touring the field, I would meet people of all ethnicities. Everyone could come and eat in that canteen. No one asked anyone what ethnicity he was or make any difficulties for people when they came, of course until the end of 1992, for as long as that source of provision of meat existed. Later on other sources were used to supply the population and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, let me go back very briefly to the relationship between your cooperative and private farmers. Did they get cattle-feed or other goods that they needed to be able to farm?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course because they would not be able to produce livestock if they were not provided regularly with cattle-feed and medicines. And the veterinary administration in Samac was in charge of the medical protection of the livestock. This went through the cooperative and the cooperative financed this supply of feed for the livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And once the livestock was bred, then the private farmer would take that livestock or the chicken or whatever, what material benefit did he have from that? Because this was a system of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, it was clearly defined by contract how much money he would receive. However, due to the shortage of funds, it was impossible to pay out compensation for his efforts, so the agreement was that he would be compensated in kind. So we would calculate how many chickens he would need in relation to the effort he and his household had invested, and then he did as best he could with what he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that this was the system applied during the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, do you perhaps know what the relationship was between the military authorities and the civilian authorities? After all, there was a war going on and there were many troops around.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning, I am not a member of any party. Of course I was not elected -- in a position to be elected to the assembly or to the executive council, where the decisions were made, but I do know that the competency was strictly divided and defined. It was known what the army did, whereas the civilian authorities regarding logistics support, that is, supplies of food and fuel and detergents and all the other essentials, were provided by the civilian administration. Also, the army required -- that is, between the civilian authorities and the army there was a standing arrangement as to how many able-bodied men could be engaged on the basis of work obligation so that the economy should continue functioning at least to some extent under abnormal conditions while at the same time that the front should not be impaired, the front line should not be short of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, regarding the achievement of tasks given to your cooperative, such as breeding of livestock, et cetera, who did this? Because some people were in the army fighting, others were under work obligation.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question. I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you who was employed in implementing the tasks assigned to your cooperative? Who were the workers there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The workers who were permanently employed and who received as their wartime assignment to work there and also temporary workers who were engaged when needed for temporary work on the basis of a decision of the Samac National Defence Department, they had to report to Agropromet or to any other organisation -- any other organisation that needed a certain number of manpower to perform its tasks. And these people who were working were compensated, as were all the -- were remunerated, as were all the other workers in Agropromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This means that you as the director of Agropromet, the farming cooperative, had insight into the people who were working there as part of their work obligation and who were remunerated for their work.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you just something else in connection with Zasavica. The gates that were manned by those two policemen that you mentioned, was there any other such police checkpoint in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in Zasavica, except for this checkpoint that you enter across the bridge and to the right-hand side there was a house where there were two policemen who took turns and there were no other checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a wire fence around the village?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, of course not. There was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And could the inhabitants of Zasavica move around freely?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The domicile population could move around the village freely. A certain number of them could leave Zasavica with permission. But large-scale freedom of movement outside Zasavica was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you went to Zasavica often, explain please how those people were accommodated, what were the conditions of life, how they were fed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the times, that is, wartime conditions, I must say that the conditions were quite exceptional, without any exaggeration, because Zasavica is a wealthy village.
