They had room -- enough room to be accommodated in. They had all necessary conditions. And they were fed with food provided to all the other population of Zasavica. And as small livestock was kept there, pigs and so on, so nobody would prevent them from slaughtering a pig and preparing for themselves a really good lunch, and so they were able to have normal meals, and there were no prohibitions of any kind set up by anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, and what was the situation with water? Was there a well there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Long ago, before the war, a well had been dug which was used to supply the whole village with water. These are Artesian wells that had been dug not just in Zasavica, in Crkvenica, Pisarevo [phoen], and a couple of villages around Zasavica. So these Artesian wells were dug long before the war in places there, including Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, and what was the situation with water in Samac itself?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: In Samac supplies were more difficult because Samac, as opposed to Zasavica where it was safer to leave because Zasavica was never shelled, Samac was frequently shelled because it was surrounded. And because of those combat operations, the town was frequently without water and of course without electricity because the electricity installations and water supply system were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions. Regarding the other kind of livestock, cows, chicken, were they available in Zasavica as well?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told you that in the Zecevic farm the capacity had 17.000 chicken in one go, in one set could be bred, so that -- in one tour. So they had this production of chicken as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And were the chicken at the disposal of the inhabitants of Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Everyone could take a chicken or two and prepare their meals, but most of it was taken from there and sent to the slaughterhouse when it was possible to reach Brcko, to slaughter the animals, and use the meat to feed the population again and the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, and what was the situation regarding vegetables and fruit? I mean in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with respect to vegetables and fruit in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: In Zasavica? Well, this was an area where vegetable-growing was developed, and they had the necessary mechanical equipment for farming. As I said, Zasavica itself was never shelled, so they could easily till their land, plant it and sow grain as well as vegetables. As for fruit, it's an expensive method of farming. There was no organised fruit-growing in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And when the time came for sowing or for harvesting or for collecting the livestock, did inhabitants of Serb ethnicity go there to work on the basis of work obligation? Were privately owned machinery engaged, tractors and combine harvesters? Were they all engaged there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. During the wheat harvest, all able-bodied men on the front and who had their own combine harvesters by decision of the Defence Ministry were given the work obligation lasting two months to harvest the wheat. And in collecting and transport Croats also took part, those who owned tractors, as did Serbs, to transport the grain to silos at the Samac combine farm -- combined farm. This supplied also in the autumn when maize and other crops were harvested. Again, they would receive from the Defence Ministry a decision on work obligation and the use of their own mechanical equipment. They even had to provide the fuel themselves because in view of a general shortage of funds the peasants themselves had to provide the fuel for the tractors and for the transport to be able to harvest the crops and store it in silos.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dujkovic. I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, I have a few questions for you. You're currently not in any party, but in 1990 you were on the list of candidates for the Alliance of Reformist Forces for Bosnia and Herzegovina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Aset Izetbegovic [phoen] was the president, and he put me on the list --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Esa Zainbegovic. I'm sorry. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you later transfer to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that I am not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I know that's the situation now, but did you later, after running for appointment with the Alliance of Reformist Forces, join the SDS for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not for a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Were you a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What rank did you hold in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I joined as captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long had you been in the 4th Detachment prior to the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the 4th Detachment at the beginning of autumn 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you attend training, take part in the administration in any way of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What role did you have in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: My role in the 4th Detachment was when the war started I was deputy company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your company?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Jovo Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And on the 16th and 17th of April, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, did the 4th Detachment undertake any operations?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the night of the 16th and 17th of April, the 4th Detachment was deployed from Pisari towards the confluence of the Bosna River to the bridge of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's during the night.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you take part in that operation?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said I was deputy company commander and I was on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So you're carrying out active operations on the night of the 16th and 17th at the -- sorry, the confluence of the Sava and what river?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The estuary, where the Bosna River flows into the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that's quite close -- in fact, it's very close to Bosanski Samac, unless I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's in Samac itself. Samac lies on the banks of two rivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you took up positions, entrenched yourselves?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no trenches dug. They were improvised, actually. We were there on the bare fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were other elements of the 4th Detachment also undertaking operations at night in addition to yours?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your company was just part of the 4th Detachment. Were other segments, other portions, other companies of the 4th Detachment also conducting operations that night?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They were on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And this -- I'm sorry to be pedantic, but this is the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And what activities were the volunteers from Serbia undertaking that night?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I was front line, I don't know what they were doing in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. But you came to know subsequently, didn't you, that they undertook operations in the town itself that night?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't even assume what they were doing because I was on the front. I cannot know what they did in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand that. I know that you were somewhere else. I understand. I heard what you said. That's not a problem. But what I'm asking you is did you subsequently come to know, later, from talking to other people, perhaps from your commanders within the 4th Detachment, what operations the Serbian paramilitaries had conducted that night?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You certainly know, don't you, that the Serbian paramilitaries also conducted operations that night in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to get me to say something that I really was not informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm up front with my questions. I'm talking about the Serbian paramilitaries, the people who came from Serbia. Certainly Lugar, Talija [phoen], men like that. You know who I'm talking about, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I had heard of Lugar and some of those people, but Lugar, for instance, has stuck in any mind. But I really don't know what they did. I really don't know what they did in Samac that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me explain it to you this way: There's been evidence in this case from numerous witnesses of the activities of the Sareni, the camouflaged ones, the Serbian paramilitaries who came in from Serbia and conducted operations on the night of the 16th and 17th of April. And Defence counsel would spring to their feet and contradict me if that was wrong. Okay? So we all know that they were conducting operations on the night of the 16th and 17th of April. There's nothing to be concerned about. Now, my question is: Did you subsequently find out what operations they were doing, performing?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I must repeat once again: I learnt that there were some people known as Sareni in town. But what operation they did, I am telling you sincerely and frankly that I really don't know what they did in the night between the 16th and 17th. Please believe me when I say this. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time after the night of the 16th and the days following, did you also engage in activity, military activity, on behalf of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was on the front line for a brief period of time from the night of the 16th to the 17th until the 5th of May, when I was appointed coordinator by a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Right. Okay. And I take it --

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: This would be roughly some ten days that I was actively involved there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Carrying out your duties as deputy commander -- deputy company commander.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, in that period of time, did the Serbian paramilitaries also conduct operations?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: You keep insisting on something that I can only tell you from what I heard, that they did commit certain operations. But what and where, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's fine. Your hearsay is fine. I'd like to know what you heard that they -- what operations you heard they were conducting.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I don't know what they were doing. They were doing something, but it -- I would be insincere if I were to say that I knew. I really don't know what they were doing between the 16th and 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But I understand what you're saying, and your position is that you don't know the details of anything that they were -- they were doing. But you do know, don't you, that they were actually carrying out military operations? You may not know what military operations, but you do know that they were conducting military operations.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can just guess at it, but I cannot explicitly say that I know that they were engaged in certain operations. I don't know. But the very fact that they were there meant that they were doing something. Now, if you're asking me what they were doing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you were engaged with an enemy, namely Croatian and Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And so were they, the Serbian paramilitaries, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were both fighting a common enemy.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And, therefore, common sense dictates that you had to coordinate your activities -- the 4th Detachment had to coordinate its activities with the Serbian paramilitaries. That must be so as a matter of common sense; don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. As I was in the 4th Detachment for a very brief period of time, there was no coordination. At least as far as the company of which I was the deputy commander is concerned there was no coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calling for speculation. This witness on numerous occasions during this testimony said that he's absolutely not aware about the details of the military arrangement of the volunteer unit and 4th Detachment, and I think my learned friend should cover another topic or another area. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I accept that the witness has testified that he doesn't know the details of any operations on the part of the paramilitaries but he knows that they were engaged in military activities. He's also a military man. He held high -- or reasonable rank in the 4th Detachment, and therefore he is in the best position to comment on any such cooperation. Now -- and so I'll proceed with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You had received training to reach the rank, I think, of major or was it captain in the reserves?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was regular training before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And you're well acquainted, aren't you, with the standard practices of any effective army, namely that there'd be hierarchy within the -- within the forces of the army?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that its operations be coordinated by commanders?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that is standard military doctrine; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And therefore, if you agree with that, and you have two military forces conducting operations in the one area against a common enemy, there must be a central command, must there not, or at least a command coordinating the operations of both forces?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: ... [End of Recording] about their specific activities. Who they coordinated activities with, if they did, please rest assured that I don't know, regardless of my rank. This is a rank as a reserve officer that one acquires undergoing certain training at a certain period of time in a certain place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand that you say you have no knowledge of the activities of the paramilitaries. I understand that. I've heard you loud and clear. I'm not asking you about their activities. I'm just asking you about basic -- the most common basic notions of military activity. Now, if you have army forces or armed forces operating against a common enemy, military doctrine requires that they be coordinated. For coordination to occur, there must be a single command. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. There must be a joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In the months that followed throughout 1992, did you have an opportunity to see the paramilitaries conducting further military operations?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I only met some of them individually, but I had no occasion of seeing their operations. I repeat, I was on the front line in the 4th Detachment for a very short period and I had a different task altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand that. You went off to Agropromet to carry out your duties. No problem. I understand that perfectly clearly. But what I'm asking is notwithstanding that, did you speak to or hear of -- speak to the paramilitaries or hear from the paramilitaries regarding their operations in the months that following April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I met Djordjevic, nicknamed Crni, who commanded the -- a special battalion. But these are not paramilitary units. These were troops engaged from among the ranks of the domicile population, and he was their commander. Therefore, he did not command any paramilitary units but a special battalion had been set up for, I presume, special tasks -- who would be engaged for some special tasks, for instance, breaking through the line, and he was their commander, but the composition of that battalion was the local population, so the troops were from the area of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's right. They were local young men specially trained and part of the special battalion and part of the Army of Republika Srpska, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And absorbed into the ranks of this special battalion were also the Serbian paramilitaries who had arrived from Serbia itself, men such as Crni, Lugar, and so on.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, in the special battalion none of the volunteers or, as you call them, paramilitaries participated in the special battalion. And as for Lugar, he act autonomously, on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. No one was able to control him; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to respond to that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What do you mean he acted autonomously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that I cannot object, but I think that perhaps it's a translation mistake. They are saying "they" in the translation booth, and the prosecutor is saying "he," and you probably referred to Lugar when you said "he," and the translation we received, the B/C/S translation, says "they," or "them as a group." So perhaps we can have this translated again to see whether the prosecutor is referring to a group or to an individual. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'll clarify it in any way. I'll just ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you saying that the man Lugar acted in the Bosanski Samac area autonomously, by himself as an individual? Is that what you're saying, or have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I said, that he acted on his own, as an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying that he was not part of this special battalion?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you agree that he was a member of the special battalion?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I told you what the concept of the special battalion was and what the -- it had been composed of. I saw but once the lads who had been recruited into the special battalion, and I never saw Lugar there. I never saw Lugar in the special battalion. But he was in Samac; that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is it your position that you don't know if he was a member of the special battalion or not?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that he was. I don't know whether he was a member of the special battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another topic, please. Zasavica, you say that there were two policemen posted there and that their job was to stop people coming in and stealing the meat and I assume also the livestock, and that was their only job.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Just -- I'm just trying to be clear. That was the sole reason that they were there, only to do that, prevent theft of livestock and meat?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I explained the basic -- their basic task was that and also apart from individual cases people could not leave the village of Zasavica in certain individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Presumably then the placing of two policemen at that point, at the little house near the bridge leading into Zasavica, was sufficient to control movement in and out of Zasavica because it would have to be, wouldn't it, in order to prevent theft?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Zasavica is not a small individual so that everything could be controlled, but this was the main road which led outside Zasavica towards Crkvina and towards Samac, and they controlled only that particular section of the road. They did not control the other directions and other exits, but then the people were not leaving. Of course, they were also concerned for their lives because men like Lugar, about whom you asked me a while ago, roamed the area of Samac uncontrolled and he could -- some people could have come to some harm or get killed. So it was just this main entrance that was placed under such control.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand that. But my point is very simple: It was a reasonably effective method of controlling movement in and out of the village.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, who were the people who weren't permitted to leave Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Zasavica, the natives, the domicile population, as well as those who had moved into Zasavica, who had come from Samac, Muslims who had taken refuge there. That is the population that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. So it was Croats, wasn't it, and Muslims who were in Zasavica who couldn't move freely in and out?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but also Serbs who had moved in subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Di Fazio, your 25 minutes are up. Do you intend to use some minutes from your account? MR. DI FAZIO: My banker, Mr. Weiner, assures me I have four minutes left. PRESIDING OFFICER: Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'll just end up on one last topic, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You described public canteens that were used to feed the army and people, and that was located in the SIT factory. And you said that the army went to feed there, to have -- to eat and also people of all ethnicities. That included, I take it, Croats -- local Croats and local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the soldiers were engaged in fighting Croat and Muslim forces, would come back from the front line for whatever reason, they would be armed and they'd go and have their lunch there.

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would have their lunch there. They would not have lunch together. When the army was there, the other people, the other population that had no other source of food, of meals, would come and eat there. And there was no one standing in the way. And that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the Croats and Muslims would happily eat side by side with the Serbian soldiers fighting Croat and Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: STANKO DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in our units there were also members of Croat and Muslim peoples, or rather, members of the Croat and Muslim ethnicities but also members of our units, apart from Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: I think that should leave us with a few minutes still in the bank, Madam Presiding Officer. PRESIDING OFFICER: That leaves you with two minutes on your account. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Dujkovic, thank you for coming today. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: We'll have a ten-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 2.54 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good afternoon, Mr. Stefanovic. Could you please stand and take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. You may sit. The Defence for Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning -- good afternoon. Will you please give me your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Dragoljub Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of October, 1979 in Samac --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, 1970. I'm very sorry. 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us please repeat this. When were you born? What is the date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of October in 1959 in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, Mr. Stefanovic, what are you by position? What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I am a construction technician, but currently I am engaged in trading and catering activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what is your marital status and do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I am married. I have two children. I have two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, Mr. Stefanovic, about -- as to one episode, so that your testifying today, as far as the Defence is concerned, will indeed be brief. Tell me, what can you tell us about the period around the 17th of April, 1992? Did you at the time meet Dragan Lukac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, whether it took place on the 17th or the day after, but it is true that I met with him and our encounter was a brief one. Before I met him, I was informed by the police at the checkpoint that they had detained Mr. Lukac, and after that I had a short encounter with him because I knew him personally from before. I worked at the Municipal Assembly of Samac, which is a building right next to the Secretariat of Internal Affairs, which is where he worked. So as I say, this meeting of ours was a short one, and I noticed when we met that he was very scared. He asked me what was going on, and at that particular moment I myself didn't know what to tell him. The police detained him, and at that moment I was in no position to influence their decisions because the work which I did had nothing to do with that particular segment of their work. So that was more or less the extent of the communication that I could have with him at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Stefanovic, where was this encounter? Where did it take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was at a cafe, at a cafe in the centre of the village which is near the checkpoint which had been erected there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else there in the company of Dragan Lukac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No one was with him at that moment. And if I recall correctly, at the time when I met him he was going out of a lavatory and I happened to pass by and that's the moment at which we met, because the place where he was temporarily detained was a building right next to that cafe and this is the trajectory, so to speak, where we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you can recall, what did Dragan Lukac physically look like on that occasion? Did you notice anything about him? Did he look normal, in other words?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you mean -- well, as I've already said, he looked frightened. I did not notice any traces of violence on his face, if that is what you meant. What I did notice is that the man was frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you tell him on that occasion that according to your information he had been arrested at the orders of Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not tell him that. The police had detained him. And as I've said a while ago, I could not influence the decisions of the police at that time. I certainly did not tell him that he had been arrested on orders from Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stefanovic. My name is Phillip Weiner, and I am a prosecutor for the Office of the Prosecutor in the ICTY. I'm going to ask you a few questions and we'll all get home today. All right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in 1990 weren't you a member of the SDS political party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your name was on the ballot in the October election for the municipal assembly, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were part of the 50 named candidates of the SDS, which included Blagoje Simic, one of the defendants in the case; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were elected to the municipal assembly, one of the 17 SDS members -- I'm sorry, 15 SDS members elected?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And not only were you elected in those 15, it was you and the defendant Blagoje Simic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was elected by the will of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew Blagoje Simic at that time and you've known him for some time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And have you remained a member of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and I am still a member today of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've continued to be an SDS member to this -- you've indicated you've continued to be an SDS member to this day; isn't that correct? That was your last answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you've continued to be an SDS member even after the three leaders of the SDS party, the three national leaders, Krajisnik, Karadzic, and Plavsic have been indicted for war crimes. You've continued to be an SDS member after those indictments; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are things which cannot associate me with that indictment. I have been a member of the League of Communists, and after the dissolution of that party, I joined the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is: You have remained a member of the SDS even though its three major leaders have been charged with war crimes to which persecution of the non-Serb population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Even after that's occurred, you've continued to be a member; isn't that true? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. For the record, it is very clear from the answer of this witness that it's not in dispute that he is a member of SDS during all times up to now. So if the Prosecution would like to establish some other grounds --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What's the basis of objection, council? Is it irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The question is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We feel it's relevant, and I ask that that not be docked from my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then -- I mean the grounds for my objection is the following: Maybe my learned friend can ask about the personal attitude of this witness towards the membership in SDS and other political issues during that period, but he already gave the answer. It's not in dispute that even during the period of indictment of these persons that you just mentioned, that he's still member. So it's absolutely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that even after those three SDS national leaders were indicted that you have -- and they're indicted for persecution of the non-Serb community in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- you have remained a member of the SDS party? Yes or no, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I consider this to be their personal responsibility. If they are to blame, if they are guilty, they will be held accountable for their personal deeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you've also remained an SDS member even after the massacre of the Muslim population -- the male Muslim population in Srebrenica in 1995 and you're still a member of the SDS party even after that, sir; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I know about these massacres only from the press, from the papers, so I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is: Even after that, you've remained an SDS member; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I'm still today a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Fine. And you're still today a member of the SDS even though one of the three SDS leaders, Biljana Plavsic, has admitted that she and fellow SDS members orchestrated a programme of persecution against the non-Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And she did that recently. And you've still maintained membership in the SDS even though she's admitted that she and the other leaders of the SDS party committed those crimes and it was their plans to commit those crimes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard that on television and in the press about this confession of hers. And as I already said, I believe that this is her personal accountability and I cannot really go into the work of the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, it's not just the work of the Tribunal. Those are the leaders of your party and the people who are making the policies. Let us move on to April 17th. Could you tell us where you -- can you tell us what you were doing on the 17th. Were you a member of any military organisation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any police unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you saw Dragan Lukac on that night of about the 17th, on that evening of about the 17th, did you keep -- at that time were you keeping a daily diary of all of your activities with -- you know some people keep a diary each day of what they see. Were you keeping a diary at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't keeping a diary, but at that time I was the commissioner because before the war started I was the president of the local commune in Crkvina, so that during these conflicts I was the commissioner. So from the post of president of the local commune in Crkvina, I became commissioner of the local commune in Crkvina, and my task was to serve as a link between the civilian authorities in Samac and the local commune or those inhabitants of the local commune who lived there but were not engaged militarily and who needed various forms of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... keep a diary, you've indicated. As part of your -- part of your position in the commune, did you file a report about this arrest that occurred of the police chief from Samac? Did you file any sort of report, written report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not consider that to be in my duty. That was within the competence of the police and it was a task for the police, and I didn't think that I ought to intervene in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if you felt it was your duty, if you felt you should have intervened, just whether or not you wrote anything down. Was there any writing that you made, a diary, a notebook, a report, anything that you listed what you had observed on that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not write anything. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when this was occurring and you were the head of the commune, you know it was a -- a very difficult time period. There was battling going on. There was shelling. There was shooting. Arrests were happening. It was a stressful period. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was by definition extremely stressful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you could -- you'd have to say it was a chaotic period. Arrests were being made. JNA troops were moving in and out of the area. There were volunteers from Serbia. A lot of things were happening at the time during that week from the 17th, let's say, to the 24th. A lot of things were happening, a chaotic stressful time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I can say that it was a chaotic time, but there were things that I had no influence on at all, things that you're referring to now, and I had other obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not saying that you were responsible or had any -- any responsibility for any of those things that happened. But if it was a chaotic time, and you agree this chaotic period that we're talking about was almost 11 years ago now that you're testifying about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This period that we're talking about, the 17th or so of -- of 1992 is almost 11 years ago; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you have no writings in relation to the activities of the evening of the 17th. Basically you're testifying strictly on the basis of your memory.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not put down anything on paper. I am testifying on the basis of what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, like people in general, all of us, you've made mistakes in your life or you've made mistakes in the past, whether it's adding numbers or saying something. You've made mistakes, like all of us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what mistakes you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Any mistakes in general, any mistake in your lifetime. Like all of us. You've added numbers incorrectly, you've made some mistake in your life --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection on the basis that this question is absolutely confusing for this witness. My learned friend should be more specific if he is speaking about certain mistakes, in which terms, when, how, et cetera. I mean, otherwise it is absolutely useless and confusing for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can 30 seconds be added to my time for that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, like everybody in this world, you've made at some point a mistake in the past. You're not perfect, like all of us; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I don't think that a perfect person exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And like all of us, you're not infallible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. This is a criminal proceedings. It is not some kind of, I would say, religious or confessional matters. We have to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Madam Presiding Officer, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- more specific. It is absolutely irrelevant and absolutely unfounded this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Madam Presiding Officer, we have rules. Objection. One word. Objection, leading; objection, irrelevant. Counsel knows the rules. Let us move on and finish the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, like all of us, you're not infallible; isn't that correct? Or do you claim to be infallible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you claiming to be infallible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You're insisting on this one question, infallible. As I have already said, there does not exist an ideal person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So like everyone else, you can make a mistake, just like everyone else; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mistakes are always possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you can make them, like everyone else? That's the question, sir. If you answer the question, we're all finished.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess so. Probably I can make a mistake. What can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a good day, sir. PRESIDING OFFICER: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The topic that I asked you today, Mr. Stefanovic, a question about your membership in the SDS, and basically the reasons which underlay in this period when Serbs and officials of the SDS were indicted, your continued membership of it and so on and so forth. I am now asking you: At the local level in Samac, did you get information that the SDS was advocating in any way the ethnic discrimination of the local population from 1992 and on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No, in no way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have to rephrase that, just in case. Yes, I will rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any personal knowledge or on the basis of any other sources have you learned that the SDS was the principal factor which conduced to the eviction -- or the moving out of the population from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... to strike. These questions are admissible if they're asked properly. These aren't proper questions. This isn't cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor asked you a question in connection with your attitude towards the SDS, et cetera. I'm now asking you: What can you tell us regarding the SDS policy to the best of your knowledge in Samac in the period in 1992 -- how would you -- 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOLJUB STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: What period did you say, 1992-1993? The party was not operating at that time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: at 3.31 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
